items.title: Christian Leaders Call America to 52 Days of Prayer and Repentance
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "It's not political."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Barbara Ann Jeter is the executive director of the Nehemiah Alliance, a movement pushing Americans toward “prayer, fasting, repentance, and national spiritual renewal.”

Jeter told CBN News the effort was birthed from an “inquiry of God last August.”

“[I asked], ‘What do you want, Lord, for America’s 250th?'” she said, noting she believes the Lord provided a path forward.

Jeter found herself sending a plan to national leaders she trusted, building the Nehemiah Alliance platform on the pattern seen in the Book of Nehemiah.

“Like Nehemiah sought the blessing of his pagan foreign king and governors along the way when he was rebuilding the walls, we have sought the blessing and gotten it from those in authority,” she said. “It’s not political, but there is something about getting the blessing of those that God’s placed in authority.”

Ultimately, Jeter was able to rally not just political leaders of the day like House Speaker Mike Johnson, but she has mobilized well-known Christian figures like Alveda King, Michael W. Smith, and Eric Metaxas, among many others, to not only support the effort but also to show up Oct. 31 for a massive event in Washington, D.C.

“We want to mobilize the people for 52 days of prayer, fasting, and repentance,” she said. “It’s historic. It’s never been done. We started Sunday on 9/10. I heard 9/11. God starts His calendar, I believe, the night before, and we’re going to All Saints Sunday. We’ll be on the National Mall. We believe it is a Nehemiah call to the wall — to the Mall — to rebuild our spiritual walls.”

Jeter said she chose Oct. 31, which is both Reformation Day and Halloween, to hold the culminating event.

“On the darkest night, we’re believing to shine the brightest light, the light of the world all over the world,” she said. “That’s Jesus.”

Even though the prayer and fasting commitment started a month ago, Jeter said it’s not too late for people to jump in now, especially since Oct. 31 is still weeks away.

“Fast as the Holy Spirit leads you,” Jeter said. “We definitely want people fasting the day of Halloween.”

In addition to prayer and fasting, she said she’s also “calling people to commit to be a modern-day gatekeeper.”

“Remember in the Bible, in Nehemiah, they built that wall in front of their own house? You’re gonna build it stronger if you’re building it in front of where you are,” she said. “Pray for your own family, your neighborhood, your local schools, your pastors. Pray for leaders and those in authority … pray for these upcoming elections.”

Jeter said she wants people to walk away from this effort with a renewed heart aimed at turning individuals, families, and culture back to Jesus. She also wants people to attend the event on the National Mall on Oct. 31.

“Come,” she said. “Answer your call to the Mall to rebuild our spiritual walls.”

items.title: Biblical Archaeology Disproves ‘Very Odd’ Claim About Modern Israel, Dinesh D’Souza Says
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "Political significance."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

As Americans’ favorability toward the modern state of Israel continues to wax and wane, as antisemitism swells, and as allegations of genocide ring out, author and commentator Dinesh D’Souza is making the case that history is on the side of the Jewish state.

Biblical archaeology, D’Souza recently told CBN News, “irrefutably shows the presence of the Jews in their ancient homeland.”

D’Souza’s comments, as well as the release of his new book, “The Stones Cry Out: Biblical Archaeology, Prophecy, and the Last Days,” come at a time when U.S. citizens are deeply divided — even in conservative and Christian circles — over Israel.

Data from the Pew Research Center shows Americans’ favorability toward both the Israeli government and its people is on the decline, with 62% holding unfavorable views toward the Jewish state’s government. Additionally, antisemitism has been on the rise in the U.S. since the Hamas-led attack against Israel in October 2023.

The Anti-Defamation League tracked a huge spike in antisemitic attacks in 2024 and, while those numbers fell somewhat in 2025, they have remained historically high. For context, the ADL recorded 6,274 incidents last year, a 33% drop from 2024 but still the third-highest total since the organization began tracking such incidents in 1979.

It’s not only an issue in America, either. Just this week, news broke of a hotel in Dublin reportedly canceling a reservation for 70 rooms for delegates attending an international conference on combating antisemitism after its administrators learned the purpose of their visit. Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland, told The Times of Israel that Herbert Park Hotel initially green-lit the booking for delegates representing the European Union’s 27 member states but later reneged after a phone call with the hotel’s general manager.

Cohen told the outlet he noticed a “manner change” in the manager after telling her the purpose of the meeting in Dublin. He recalled a “tension that had not been there before” when, upon learning the purpose of the event, the general manager asked Cohen if the Israel Defense Forces would be involved in the gathering.

“We were talking about a conference in Dublin on antisemitism, attended by Jewish community representatives, diplomats, civil servants and government officials,” he told The Times. “Nothing I had said had anything whatsoever to do with the Israeli army, yet, somehow, that was where the conversation had gone.”

The manager then purportedly told Cohen she’d have to check with the owners to determine whether the reservation could remain. Apparently, it could not: the rooms were canceled.

Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, told Fox News the incident “is a disgraceful example of the very antisemitism the conference was organized to combat.”

Much of the hostility toward Israel centers on the claim the Jewish state is committing genocide against Palestinians, a leftist talking point becoming less defensible as new data from the Palestinian Ministry of Health shows the population in Gaza actually grew significantly in 2025. Nevertheless, as CBN News reported, Israel remains on high alert against attacks ahead of its Oct. 27 elections.

D’Souza, for his part, made the case this week that it’s “very odd” to accuse Israelis of seeking to take land that does not belong to them when there is a breadth of archaeological history proving Jewish presence in the land dating back centuries.

“It really irrefutably shows the presence of the Jews in their ancient homeland, going back 3,000, even more than 3,000 years,” he said. “And so the familiar accusation that the Jews are colonizers immediately becomes very odd, right? Because it’s like accusing the Indians of colonizing India or the Irish of colonizing Ireland. How do you colonize your own ancestral homeland?”

To make his case, D’Souza pointed to a 2,000-year-old, 25-ton Jewish ritual bath, known as a mikveh, discovered this summer by the Israel Antiquities Authority. The relic, which was excavated nearly totally intact, provides evidence of a previously unknown Jewish settlement between the Judean Lowlands and the northern Negev, according to the IAA.

“[T]hese ritual baths were used by Jews to kind of cleanse themselves before they went to the temple,” D’Souza explained. “So there is a political significance, I think, to these archaeological exhibits coming out of the ground.”

items.title: Financial Anxiety Doesn’t Care How Much You Make
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: The paycheck lands. The balance goes up. The knot in your stomach doesn’t move. If that’s your Friday, you’ve got company. In The Motley Fool’s 2026 Financial Anxiety and Mental Health Survey, 52 percent of American millennials rated their money stress as high or extremely high. More than a third sa
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

The paycheck lands. The balance goes up. The knot in your stomach doesn’t move.

If that’s your Friday, you’ve got company. In The Motley Fool’s 2026 Financial Anxiety and Mental Health Survey, 52 percent of American millennials rated their money stress as high or extremely high. More than a third said they feel it five or more days a week. Half said it has wrecked their sleep, and 45 percent said it fed into anxiety, depression or another diagnosis.

Here’s the number that should get your attention, though. Among people earning more than $100,000 a year, 38 percent still described their stress as high. The raise didn’t fix it.

“Financial anxiety exists at every income level,” says Paige Whitaker, brand growth and partnerships manager at 316 Financial, a faith-forward bank. “Some people are anxious because they don’t have enough. Others are anxious because they’re afraid of losing what they have. More money alone doesn’t always solve the problem.”

What It’s Actually Costing You

Money stress rarely stays in the bank app. It shows up as the 2 a.m. ceiling stare, the snippy text about the Venmo request, the job you keep because leaving feels like jumping without a net. The survey put numbers on it: 41 percent said financial stress has made it harder to enjoy daily life, 37 percent reported physical symptoms like headaches and fatigue, and 22 percent skipped a doctor or dentist appointment because of the cost.

A third of people also said they’re uncomfortable talking about any of it with friends or family. So the thing eating at you is also the thing you’re carrying alone.

“Financial anxiety is about far more than dollars and cents,” Whitaker says. “It impacts our relationships, our health, our decision-making, and even our spiritual lives. When we’re constantly worrying about money, it’s difficult to experience the peace that God intends for us.”

Fear Is a Bad Lens

Whitaker’s read on why it hits so hard comes down to uncertainty. “We want guarantees about the future, but life rarely works that way,” she says. “The challenge is that when fear becomes our primary lens, we begin making decisions based on panic instead of wisdom.”

Panic decisions look like not opening the bill because you already know it’s bad. Putting the whole emergency on a card and dealing with it later. Saying yes to the side gig you hate because saying no felt reckless. None of those are dumb. They’re what a scared brain does. The trouble is that fear is a terrible financial planner, and its decisions compound.

The Part Where Faith Comes In

Christians have a complicated relationship with this one. We know the verses. Philippians 4:6-7, don’t be anxious about anything. 1 Peter 5:7, cast your anxiety on him because he cares for you. And then we feel guilty for being anxious anyway, which just adds a layer.

Markeia Johnson, who leads the Financial Stewardship Committee at 316 Financial, says those passages are an invitation, and they come with a catch people miss. “These Scriptures assure us that we don’t have to carry financial burdens alone,” she says. “Trusting God does not mean neglecting financial responsibility. Wise stewardship, budgeting and planning remain important, but faith allows us to rely on God’s wisdom rather than fear.”

Read that twice. Trusting God and keeping a budget go together. One deals with the fear. The other deals with the facts.

Three Moves That Actually Help

Name the specific fear. “I’m bad with money” is a mood. “If my car dies I have $400 and no plan” is a problem, and problems can be worked. Write the worst case down. Most of the time it’s survivable, and seeing it on paper takes some of the charge out.

Do the boring thing anyway. A budget is a fear-reduction tool. Knowing the number is almost always less stressful than guessing the number, even when the number is bad. Automate what you can so you’re not re-deciding every month.

Separate your security from your net worth. This is the faith move, and it’s the one money can’t do for you. “By choosing prayer over panic and trusting God through uncertainty, we can experience peace that is rooted not in our circumstances, but in His presence and provision,” Johnson says.

None of that makes the bill smaller. It changes who’s making your decisions.

“Financial anxiety doesn’t just drain our wallets. It drains our peace,” Whitaker says. “When we place our ultimate security in money, we’ll never feel like we have enough. When we place our trust in God, we can pursue financial health without being consumed by fear.”

items.title: The Coin Belongs to Caesar, But Caeser Belongs to God
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, on this Twenty-ninth Sunday of the year, our Gospel features the question from the Pharisees about paying taxes.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, on this Twenty-ninth Sunday of the year, our Gospel features the question from the Pharisees about paying taxes. In response to the trap, Jesus offers one of the most famous one-liners in history: “Repay to Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God what belongs to God.” His answer didn’t automatically solve the problem of the relationship between church and state, but it did point the way through two opposite extremes, both of which are predicated on a false understanding of how God relates to the world.

Daily Reading

First Reading
Isaiah 45:1, 4-6

Thus says the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus,
    whose right hand I have grasped
to subdue nations before him
    and strip kings of their robes,
to open doors before him—
    and the gates shall not be closed:
For the sake of my servant Jacob,
    and Israel my chosen,
I call you by your name,
    I surname you, though you do not know me.
I am the Lord, and there is no other;
    besides me there is no god.
    I arm you, though you do not know me,
so that they may know, from the rising of the sun
    and from the west, that there is no one besides me;
    I am the Lord, and there is no other.

Psalm
Psalm 96:1, 3, 4-5, 7-8, 9-10

O sing to the Lord a new song;
    sing to the Lord, all the earth.
Declare his glory among the nations,
    his marvelous works among all the peoples.
For great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised;
    he is to be revered above all gods.
For all the gods of the peoples are idols,
    but the Lord made the heavens.
For great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised;
    he is to be revered above all gods.
For all the gods of the peoples are idols,
    but the Lord made the heavens.
Worship the Lord in holy splendor;
    tremble before him, all the earth.
Say among the nations, “The Lord is king!
    The world is firmly established; it shall never be moved.
    He will judge the peoples with equity.”

Second Reading
1 Thessalonians 1:1-5b

 Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy,

To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ:

Grace to you and peace.

We always give thanks to God for all of you and mention you in our prayers, constantly remembering before our God and Father your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ. For we know, brothers and sisters beloved by God, that he has chosen you, because our message of the gospel came to you not in word only, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction; just as you know what kind of persons we proved to be among you for your sake.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 22:15-21

Then the Pharisees went and plotted to entrap him in what he said. So they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that you are sincere, and teach the way of God in accordance with truth, and show deference to no one; for you do not regard people with partiality. Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to the emperor, or not?” But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, “Why are you putting me to the test, you hypocrites? Show me the coin used for the tax.” And they brought him a denarius. Then he said to them, “Whose head is this, and whose title?” They answered, “The emperor’s.” Then he said to them, “Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

items.title: Pursuing ‘Sense’ and ‘Sensibility’ in Catholic Dating
items.author: Nora Kenney Mittiga
items.summary:
Nora Kenney Mittiga

Two centuries after Austen diagnosed the problem, we have no shortage of good advice for avoiding romantic delusion.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Nora Kenney Mittiga

What Jane Austen’s original “delulu girl” can teach us about romance, reality, and vocation

The women of Gen Z have once again done a service to society by giving us (among many other useful terms, like “pick-me girl,” “theatre kid,” and “Disney adult”) the word “delulu.” A humorous abbreviation of “delusional,” it captures a specific kind of female romantic derangement—especially that which emerges wherever men, mixed signals, and wishful thinking converge. Millennials had the phrase “He’s just not that into you,” the title of a 2004 book and 2009 movie. But Gen Z has the catchier, more brutal diagnosis: “delulu.”

This week, audiences will get reacquainted with one of literature’s most iconic delulu girls in a new film adaptation of Jane Austen’s 1811 classic, Sense and Sensibility. In her debut novel, Austen compares two sisters with two radically different ways of navigating love: the restrained, prudent Elinor Dashwood and the romantic, impulsive Marianne. The 2026 version, directed by Georgia Oakley, stars Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor and Esme Creed-Miles as Marianne, and arrives in theaters October 16. 

In anticipation of the new adaptation, it’s worth revisiting Austen’s treatment of romantic self-deception and considering it alongside Gen Z’s delulu-girl archetype. Dating advice is having something of a renaissance, and much of it—from the rising (and surprising) popularity of Laura Doyle to Arthur Brooks’s recent prescriptions for finding a spouse—is surprisingly reasonable and relevant (especially for Catholics, who should be approaching the concept of vocation seriously). With that in mind, Austen’s original delulu girl offers a useful test case for how much we’ve learned about the difference between romantic hope and wishful fantasy in the 215 years since the book came out. 

Without getting too deeply into spoilers, Marianne’s problems begin when she falls headlong for the charming John Willoughby (much like Lydia Bennet for George Wickham in Austen’s most famous book, Pride and Prejudice) and allows the intensity of the attachment (what modern audiences would call a “situationship”) to cloud her thinking. Their chemistry is obvious, and the understanding between the two seems complete. After all, Marianne is receiving all the signals—the brooding eye contact, the clandestine excursions, the obsequious appeals to her mother—except the one that would actually indicate commitment by her generation’s standards: a proposal. Instead, much like Wickham, Willoughby starts to seem like what Gen Z would call a “walking red flag.” In other words, what Willoughby leads Marianne to believe about their dynamic begins to outrun what he is actually promising her, or what the material evidence of his intentions is revealing. 

Kate Winslet captures the resulting devastation magnificently in Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation—and we’ll soon see if Creed-Miles can equally deliver. When Marianne is finally forced to acknowledge the gap between the romance she believed herself to be living and the reality of Willoughby’s intentions—to acknowledge, in contemporary parlance, that she’s been “breadcrumbed”—her grief is all-consuming. Winslet’s reaction is so complete—so bodily and operatic—that the effect is simultaneously heartbreaking and, in the way romantic catastrophes can be only when viewed from the outside, a little tragically, guiltily hilarious. (Anyone who has ever watched a delulu friend insist that the mixed signals she is receiving in a situationship are actually perfectly clear—and, like Miranda watching Carrie with Mr. Big in Sex and the City, a favorite among Gen Z, wanted to shake her by the shoulders—will recognize the feeling.)

But what would Laura Doyle and Arthur Brooks say? Thankfully, a new generation of dating advice is also gently advising women to snap out of it. And, controversial as it may be to say so, this type of “tough love” is particularly vital for Catholic daters, who are wasting precious, finite time. Of course, complications happen, but none of us has infinite time to discern and pursue our vocations—though we certainly all have an obligation to do so—especially if that vocation may entail being fruitful and multiplying in a physical sense. We should therefore be good stewards of the time we’ve been given, being especially wary of squandering it on irresponsible—dare we say, self-indulgent—delulu fancies. 

A recent feature in The New York Times profiles Laura Doyle, a contrarian relationship guru who’s ruffled feathers—and gained a cult following—with her retrograde advice for women in difficult relationships. (She offers such old-school wisdom as stop nagging, stop micromanaging, and most provocatively, “surrender” control within marriage.) But while the Times largely focused on Doyle’s advice for married women, the Californian has also written widely about dating, and her insights in that area are similarly countercultural: relinquish control of the courtship’s outcome, let a man pursue you, and stop trying to coax affection or commitment where it doesn’t exist. If he is flirting with you but not actually committing, be realistic about what you’re seeing. Becoming fixated on someone who is not committing risks potentially missing legitimate opportunities altogether. Whether applied to dating or marriage, a common thread of Doyle’s wisdom is stop trying to manipulate reality into what you want it to be. In other words: don’t be delulu. 

Social scientist and “happiness expert” Dr. Arthur Brooks has also been wading into the world of dating advice. In a recent piece for The Free Press, he wrote, provocatively, “Dating Apps Aren’t Broken. You’re Just Using Them Wrong.” Would that this message could be plastered on the billboards or subway walls along the commutes of all ultra-picky delulu girls everywhere. Brooks’s main takeaway is that while most young people want love, they often screen potential partners for the wrong qualities. Instead of overvaluing superficial markers of compatibility (like chemistry, excitement, “sparks,” and explosive “fireworks”—all qualities Marianne seeks), Brooks advises seeking the traits that actually predict a good long-term mate: honesty, conscientiousness, agreeableness, and crucially, a clearly stated desire for commitment. These traits may be a little less “sexy” than, say, those driving the tortured dynamic between Jane and the “Byronic hero,” Mr. Rochester in Jane Eyre (another Austen-adjacent classic). But they translate into “durable pair-bond mating for survival, growth, and development of family,” or as Brooks puts it, “all the stuff you say you want in your wedding vows.” In other words, stop falling for the idea of a man (or simply the one who elicits “butterflies”) and start paying attention to the evidence of his character and intentions—data points that may require giving someone a few shy, uncomfortable dates (rather than cutting him off after one) to fully evaluate. This is, again, another way of saying: don’t be delulu.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Rachael Sherrill, a lesser-known dating and relationship coach—another blonde from California—actually puts it best. In a YouTube video that should be required watching for every Catholic woman starting at age eighteen, Sherrill explains what she calls “the dating strategy of the decade.” The strategy sounds like it should be common-sense. But again, in this age of breadcrumbing and situationships (and Austen’s apparently), it isn’t, insofar as it requires slaying the sacred cow of delusion. “When you are dating, from here on out, I want you girls to get into the habit of becoming most available for the guys that give you the most attention. Are you tracking with me?” she asks. “And then I want you to become the most unavailable person for men who are not giving you attention, who are giving you breadcrumbs, who give you a little and then pull back, give you a little, then they’re not there.” She continues, “Guys who are leaving you breadcrumbs, I want you to become uninterested in. And for the guys who are actually showing attention and intention to you and towards you, I want you to become available.” 

Sherrill has said elsewhere on social media that this advice is difficult for women to absorb because they’re conditioned to want unavailable men—what we might, again, call the Byronic hero (the brooding, emotionally unavailable type). But Sherrill attributes women’s tendency to discount the attention of generous, consistent, stable men to issues of self-confidence and unresolved wounds that can be addressed and healed, allowing them to recalibrate what—and whom—they find attractive.

Matthew Hussey also fits this category. One of his recurring admonitions is deceptively simple: “Attention is not intention.” Like Willoughby, a man can text you, flirt with you, enjoy spending time with you, and shower you with attention without actually intending to build a future with you. Instead, try to “value character as much as you value chemistry,” Hussey says—to look beyond the intoxicating sparks of attraction and ask whether the person in front of you is actually honest, loyal, kind, and capable of following through. In other words, attention is not commitment and chemistry is not character; “the false love stories we tell ourselves about situations that don’t actually represent any real potential” should not be mistaken for evidence of relationships that do not yet exist. 

Doyle, Brooks, Sherrill, and Hussey are all offering excellent (albeit tough) advice. If only Marianne could have scrolled through Instagram (in between traipsing wistfully through the English countryside—admittedly a better use of time for other reasons) and found their work before meeting Willoughby. And if only the delulus of this day and age would listen. 

Today, it’s discussed ad nauseam in certain public-policy circles, but the West’s marriage and birth rates are concerningly low. This is happening even among Catholics. As a new report from the Institute for Family Studies points out, the number of Catholic weddings in the United States has plummeted by 74 percent since 1970, from 415,000 to just 109,000 in 2024. Contributing to this dynamic of declining marriage rates is the fact that, frustrated with breadcrumbing and situationships, some women are entering their secular “celibacy eras,” opting out of dating altogether. Others remain hopelessly delulu, holding out for romantic fantasies nourished by some combination of the Disney Princess-industrial complex and a lingering cultural weakness for the brooding (read: “avoidant”) Byronic hero. Neither response is particularly conducive to finding and forming stable marriages. If we want to push back against these tendencies, the growing cohort of anti-delulu dating coaches is a surprisingly good place to start. 

This takes on added weight for Catholics. Catholics are called to discern and live a vocation—to foster an attitude of “vigilance and a conscious attentiveness to the voice of God” and what he wants of our lives, as John Paul II wrote in 1988’s Christifideles Laici. A Catholic should aim to figure out quickly what that vocation is. (“The fundamental objective of the formation of the lay faithful is an ever-clearer discovery of one’s vocation and the ever-greater willingness to live it so as to fulfil one’s mission,” he continues in the same document). Catholics should ask themselves first if the vocation might be to religious life. If not—if and when a young person discerns that he or she is called to marriage—he or she should be serious, not delusional, about finding a spouse. That spouse shouldn’t be someone who repulses the discerner, of course, but to be overly fixated on chemistry—on the “soulmate myth,” as Brad Wilcox puts it—is to make an idol of romance. “A vocation—any vocation—is a school of charity and a means of crucifixion,” writes Benjamin Mann in a blogpost aptly titled “Discernment Is Not About You.” 

Paradoxically, then, dating does not have to be the most romantic process in the entire world, just one of obedience. After all, “Your vocation is not the answer to the question of your being; it is only a part of God’s pledge that the answer will be given in the end,” Mann writes. Thus, Catholics should not idolize romance and chemistry. Instead, they should pursue self-giving marital love—which can be a little bit more boring than a volatile Hollywood romance, perhaps, but also a lot more stable and self-giving—not only for one’s spouse, but also for the surrounding community, who are counting on them to have children, raise good kids, and be a witness to Christ’s love with their marriage. 

And the fruits of such sanctifying obedience can be rapturously surprising. A young priest in Minnesota recently had a mystical experience while celebrating Mass: an intense sense of Christ’s presence during the consecration of the Precious Blood. Surely every day of his priesthood does not feel like that—much of it presumably feels like the mundane, repetitive fidelity to any vocation. But on that particular day, extraordinary grace broke through in the midst of ordinary vocational obedience. That type of mystical encounter with the other side of the veil is not promised to anyone, but it is a reminder that faithfulness and obedience to one’s vocation can open onto realities far more ecstatic than the “Hollywood” feelings we are so tempted to demand at the outset. 

All hope is not lost for single Catholics, contemporary delulu girls, or even for Marianne. As viewers of the Oakley version will hopefully soon see, there are good options—men of good character—who can be obscured when a delulu girl’s mind is clouded, only to come into view once she undergoes a reality check (usually administered by a tough-love sister or girlfriend). We can only assume Oakley will do justice to this dynamic, but viewers will have to watch the movie to find out. In the meantime, the fact remains: Two centuries after Austen diagnosed the problem, we have no shortage of good advice for avoiding romantic delusion. And life on the other side of being delulu can be pretty good—even lavishly abundant—with the graces that come from obedience to God’s call.
